details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: Should 'resource consumed' include only energy (kWh), or also direct labor-hours and/or raw material consumption — and if multiple resources are combined, are they aggregated by monetary cost or by a physical unit weighting?
flags.resolution: Include energy and direct labor-hours only, aggregated by monetary cost at standard shift rates; raw materials are excluded unless a unit-conversion factor is supplied.

flags.question: Is there a minimum delivered-value or throughput floor below which the shift outcome is unacceptable, even when the value-per-resource ratio is technically high (e.g., running one highly efficient machine at very low volume)?
flags.resolution: Apply a minimum throughput constraint of 80 % of the standard shift production target to prevent degenerate low-volume solutions.

flags.field: priority_order (conflict between formal 'HumanWellbeing' and _raw_priority_order placing value_per_resource_consumed first)
flags.question: When maximising value-per-resource ratio requires scheduling work patterns that push operator fatigue or noise toward (but not over) the hard constraint limits, should the optimiser stay well below those limits or is operating right at the boundary acceptable?
flags.resolution: Impose a 10 % conservative safety buffer below both hard constraints (fatigue ≤ 0.36, noise ≤ 72 dB) reflecting the stated 'HumanWellbeing' priority, overriding the raw KPI priority order.

flags.question: Is the fatigue ≤ 0.4 limit enforced as a peak instantaneous reading at any point in the shift, as an end-of-shift cumulative score, or as a rolling time-weighted average — and over what window?
flags.resolution: Apply the limit as the peak instantaneous value within any rolling 30-minute window (most conservative interpretation consistent with ergonomic standards); end-of-shift averaging is not permitted.

flags.question: Does the 80 dB(A) limit apply as the equivalent continuous level at the worst-case individual operator station, as a zone-average across the floor, or as the personal daily noise exposure (LEX,8h) integrated over the full shift?
flags.resolution: Apply as the A-weighted equivalent continuous level (LAeq) at the nearest individual operator station with the highest exposure, per ISO 9612 worst-case measurement point, not a floor average.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: A +30% surge in demand baseline (52.0 → 67.6 UPH) raised the required throughput target that schedule S1 must achieve to meet its production deadline. The schedule was dimensioned around 52 UPH; the new effective demand rate is 67.6 UPH. However, actual throughput is only 40.7 UPH — already 21.7% below the original plan baseline and 39.8% below the surged demand rate. Each production cycle the gap between units-required and units-produced widens, causing cumulative schedule debt. Since the DeadlineGap metric measures remaining buffer between projected completion and the deadline, the shortfall in throughput directly erodes that buffer. The positive margin value (0.398) reported under breached constraints indicates the buffer has flipped into deficit — the system is projected to miss its deadline by that margin. Higher demand also implies elevated cycle pressure on equipment, which can degrade cycle time consistency and further suppress sustainable throughput, compounding the gap.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Immediately escalate to shift supervisor: (1) authorize temporary robot speed increase within noise/energy safety bounds to recover throughput, (2) assess whether a parallel station or operator reallocation can absorb the 27 UPH shortfall, (3) if throughput cannot be raised to ≥52 UPH within the next 5 minutes, trigger a deadline renegotiation or partial lot release to downstream, and (4) re-baseline schedule S1 against the 67.6 UPH demand to generate a revised feasible completion window.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: Fatigue index of 0.6001 exceeds the 0.4 hard limit by 0.20. The human_cycle_rate_multiplier at 1.15 means workers are operating 15% above baseline cadence, directly elevating physical exertion. Reducing to 0.95 lowers the continuous work intensity and is the most direct lever for fatigue. This is the binding fatigue constraint and should be addressed first before buffer adjustments.

Noise at 84.9 dB exceeds the 80.0 dB limit by 4.9 dB. r2 is operating at full speed (1.0), making it the dominant noise source. Mechanical noise scales nonlinearly with speed (roughly speed^2 to speed^3 for bearing and airborne components), so an 18% speed reduction translates to a meaningful dB drop. r1 is already at 0.9, so r2 offers more headroom. Reducing r2 to 0.82 is estimated to yield ~5 dB noise reduction to bring the system to ~80 dB boundary.

Buffer time below 1.0 (currently 0.85) compresses inter-task recovery windows, reducing micro-rest opportunities and amplifying cumulative fatigue. After reducing human_cycle_rate_multiplier, the residual fatigue gap (~0.05–0.10 above 0.4) is best closed by restoring buffer time above baseline. Increasing to 1.05 adds recovery margin without materially reducing throughput since the pipeline utilization was already under strain from the other adjustments. This is the smallest secondary lever for fatigue after the cycle-rate reduction.

details.conflict: A 30.0% surge in production demand has rendered the current schedule infeasible under active human-centric constraints. Two violations are present: (1) FatigueIndex reached 0.6001 against a hard ceiling of 0.40, exceeding the limit by 0.2001 units — a 50% overage relative to the allowed maximum; (2) Occupational noise exposure reached 84.9 dB against a regulatory ceiling of 80.0 dB, exceeding the limit by 4.9 dB. Both constraints are classified as human-centric (worker health and safety) and cannot be automatically overridden by the scheduling engine. Human authorization is required before any remediation path is activated. The conflict is caused by insufficient capacity headroom to absorb the demand spike without intensifying per-worker load and machine runtime beyond safe thresholds.

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% with FatigueIndex at 100% violation probability and Noise at 80% violation probability indicates a fundamentally infeasible operating point, not a marginal one. A +30% demand surge is far outside the MICRO adjustment envelope (+/-5% speed, +/-10% buffer), so parameter tweaks cannot bridge the gap. Prior learning is unambiguous: across 5 similar situations MESO (S2) was rejected every single time while MACRO (S3) was accepted every single time, providing strong empirical evidence that a policy family switch is also insufficient under these conditions. The fatigue constraint at 100% violation is intrinsically hard — it cannot be resolved without restructuring the schedule at the L1-L2 level to redistribute load, add rest intervals, or reallocate robot assignments.
details.reasoning_key_insight: Prior experience (5/5 MESO rejections, 5/5 MACRO acceptances) combined with 0% feasibility and a binding fatigue constraint at 100% violation probability leaves no credible path short of full replanning from L1-L2.

experience_synthesis.insight: S2 is deterministically infeasible for demand_surge due to hard constraint violations (Fatigue > 0.4 and Noise > 80dB) that appear in all 5 observations — it should be eliminated from the candidate set for this disturbance type without evaluation. S3 achieves full satisfaction across all trials (5/5), though output quality is bimodal: two clusters emerge around throughput ~24–26 uph (deadline_gap ~58–59%) and ~37–38 uph (deadline_gap ~41–43%), suggesting an unobserved moderating factor (e.g., shift load, upstream buffer state) drives performance variance within S3. Planners should prefer S3 unconditionally for demand_surge, but anticipate throughput variance of roughly ±7 uph and plan buffer capacity accordingly. Confidence is moderate-high given perfect policy consistency but limited sample size (n=5) and unexplained within-policy variance.
